body:
## What Is Keigo?

⟦{敬語|けいご}→敬語：04022_keigo⟧ (keigo) is the Japanese honorific language system. It is not just about being "polite" — it is a structured system for expressing social relationships through language. Keigo shows respect for the listener, humility about yourself, or general politeness in formal situations.

Using keigo correctly is essential in workplaces, formal interactions, and when speaking with people you do not know well. Even intermediate learners encounter keigo frequently in daily life — at shops, restaurants, and in business settings.

## The Three Types

### 1. ⟦{尊敬語|そんけいご}→尊敬語：17106_sonkeigo⟧ — Respectful Language

Used to elevate the actions of the person you are speaking about (your boss, a customer, a stranger). You use ⟦{尊敬語|そんけいご}→尊敬語：17106_sonkeigo⟧ when describing what someone of higher status does.

**Formation patterns:**
- お + verb stem + ⟦に→に：00314_ni⟧⟦なる→なる：01970_naru⟧: お⟦{読|よ}み→読む：00426_yomu⟧⟦に→に：00314_ni⟧⟦なる→なる：01970_naru⟧ (to read — respectful)
- Special replacement verbs: ⟦いらっしゃる→いらっしゃる：01295_irassharu⟧, ⟦おっしゃる→おっしゃる：01299_ossharu⟧, ⟦{召|め}し{上|あ}がる→召し上がる：01310_meshiagaru⟧
- ～れる / ～られる (passive form used as light honorific)

### 2. ⟦{謙譲語|けんじょうご}→謙譲語：15869_kenjougo⟧ — Humble Language

Used to lower your own actions relative to the listener. You use ⟦{謙譲語|けんじょうご}→謙譲語：15869_kenjougo⟧ when describing what you or your in-group does.

**Formation patterns:**
- お + verb stem + ⟦する→する：00392_suru⟧: お⟦{持|も}ち→持つ：00478_motsu⟧⟦する→する：00392_suru⟧ (to carry — humble)
- Special replacement verbs: ⟦いたす→いたす：01314_itasu⟧, ⟦{申|もう}す→申す：01319_mousu⟧, ⟦{参|まい}る→参る：01322_mairu⟧

### 3. ⟦{丁寧語|ていねいご}→丁寧語：15824_teineigo⟧ — Polite Language

The most familiar form for learners: です and ます endings. ⟦{丁寧語|ていねいご}→丁寧語：15824_teineigo⟧ does not elevate or lower anyone — it simply makes speech polite and appropriate for formal situations.

## Common Verb Transformations

The table below shows how everyday verbs change in each keigo type:

| Plain | Meaning | Respectful (⟦{尊敬語|そんけいご}→尊敬語：17106_sonkeigo⟧) | Humble (⟦{謙譲語|けんじょうご}→謙譲語：15869_kenjougo⟧) |
|-------|---------|------------|--------|
| ⟦{行|い}く→行く：00119_iku⟧ / ⟦{来|く}る→来る：00254_kuru⟧ | go / come | ⟦いらっしゃる→いらっしゃる：01295_irassharu⟧, ⟦おいでになる→おいでになる：01631_oideninaru⟧ | ⟦{参|まい}る→参る：01322_mairu⟧ |
| ⟦いる→いる：00495_iru⟧ | be (exist) | ⟦いらっしゃる→いらっしゃる：01295_irassharu⟧ | ⟦おる→おる：01324_oru⟧ |
| ⟦{食|た}べる→食べる：00396_taberu⟧ / ⟦{飲|の}む→飲む：00322_nomu⟧ | eat / drink | ⟦{召|め}し{上|あ}がる→召し上がる：01310_meshiagaru⟧ | ⟦いただく→いただく：01326_itadaku⟧ |
| ⟦{言|い}う→言う：00515_iu⟧ | say | ⟦おっしゃる→おっしゃる：01299_ossharu⟧ | ⟦{申|もう}す→申す：01319_mousu⟧, ⟦{申|もう}し{上|あ}げる→申し上げる：01734_moushiageru⟧ |
| ⟦する→する：00392_suru⟧ | do | ⟦なさる→なさる：01307_nasaru⟧ | ⟦いたす→いたす：01314_itasu⟧ |
| ⟦{見|み}る→見る：00283_miru⟧ | see | ⟦ご{覧|らん}になる→ご覧になる：01311_goranninaru⟧ | ⟦{拝見|はいけん}する→拝見する：01823_haikensuru⟧ |
| ⟦くれる→くれる：00724_kureru⟧ | give (to me) | ⟦くださる→くださる：01305_kudasaru⟧ | — |
| あげる | give | — | ⟦{差|さ}し{上|あ}げる→差し上げる：01597_sashiageru⟧ |
| ⟦{知|し}る→知る：00458_shiru⟧ | know | ⟦ご{存|ぞん}じ→ご存じ：01594_gozonji⟧ | ⟦{存|ぞん}じる→存じる：05912_zonjiru⟧ |

## When to Use Each Type

**Use ⟦{尊敬語|そんけいご}→尊敬語：17106_sonkeigo⟧ when talking about:**
- Your boss or supervisor
- Customers or clients
- Older people you do not know well
- Teachers and professors

**Use ⟦{謙譲語|けんじょうご}→謙譲語：15869_kenjougo⟧ when talking about:**
- Yourself in formal situations
- Your own company or family (when speaking to outsiders)
- Actions you perform for someone of higher status

**Use ⟦{丁寧語|ていねいご}→丁寧語：15824_teineigo⟧ (です/ます) when:**
- Speaking to anyone you are not close friends with
- In any public or semi-formal situation
- As a default safe choice when unsure

## Common Mistakes

1. **Using respectful forms for yourself.** Saying ⟦いらっしゃいます→いらっしゃる：01295_irassharu⟧ about your own actions is a common learner error. Respectful forms are for others; use humble forms for yourself.

2. **Mixing levels inconsistently.** Switching between casual and keigo within the same conversation (to the same person) sounds unnatural. Choose a level and maintain it.

3. **Over-using keigo in casual settings.** Using full keigo with close friends sounds stiff and distant. Save it for appropriate contexts.

4. **Double honorifics.** Stacking two respectful forms on one verb, as in ⟦おっしゃられる→おっしゃる：01299_ossharu⟧ (⟦おっしゃる→おっしゃる：01299_ossharu⟧ plus られる) or ⟦ご{覧|らん}→ご覧：01408_goran⟧⟦に→に：00314_ni⟧⟦なられる→なる：01970_naru⟧, is redundant and sounds awkward. A few doubled forms have become accepted through long use, notably ⟦お{召|め}し{上|あ}がり→お召し上がり：26515_omeshiagari⟧⟦に→に：00314_ni⟧⟦なる→なる：01970_naru⟧ and ⟦お{見|み}えになる→お見えになる：17274_omieninaru⟧, but they are exceptions, not a pattern to copy.

## Tips for Learners

1. **Master です/ます first.** This is the most widely useful level and the foundation for all keigo.
2. **Learn the irregular verbs.** The special keigo verbs (⟦いらっしゃる→いらっしゃる：01295_irassharu⟧, ⟦おっしゃる→おっしゃる：01299_ossharu⟧, etc.) are used constantly — memorize them as vocabulary items.
3. **Listen at workplaces and shops.** Keigo is everywhere in Japanese service culture. Pay attention to how staff speak to customers.
4. **When in doubt, use です/ます.** It is always safer to be slightly too polite than too casual.
5. **Read the companion articles.** [Greetings and Set Phrases for Everyday Life](greetings.html) shows keigo inside the fixed phrases of daily life, and [Referring to People](referring-to-people.html) covers the names, titles, and family terms that go with it.
